Once again, minerals worth $500 billion for the United States. According to the Budapest Memorandum (1994), Ukraine gave up the world's third largest nuclear arsenal in exchange for security guarantees from the United States, the United Kingdom, and Russia.
List of nuclear weapons that Ukraine has transferred to Russia or destroyed:
1. Nuclear warheads - about 1900 units (strategic and tactical).
2. Intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) RS-18 “Stiletto” (SS-19) and RS-22 “Scalpel” (SS-24) - 176 units.
3. Strategic bombers:
Tu-160 - 19 pcs.
Tu-95MS - 25 pcs.
Tu-22M3 - 60 units (partly utilized, partly transferred to Russia).
4. Nuclear cruise missiles X-55 - about 1100 units.
5. Launchers for intercontinental ballistic missiles - 130 silo launchers.
6. Nuclear weapons control and communication systems.
Estimates of the value of the transferred nuclear arsenal vary, but in general, Ukraine has lost at least $250-300 billion worth of weapons in 1990s prices. If we translate this amount into modern prices, the cost could be more than $500-600 billion.
What did Ukraine get in return?
Financial compensation: about $500 million from the United States.
Supply of nuclear fuel for Ukrainian NPPs in the approximate amount of USD 1 billion.
Security guarantees, which, as the 2014-2022 war showed, were not fulfilled. (tens or hundreds of thousands killed and maimed)
Instead, Ukraine lost its nuclear status and became a victim of Russia's military aggression.

comments.text:
Western tanks have better optics than Russian tanks, and significantly better than the old Russian tanks being pulled out of storage. It also helps that western tanks can are much quicker in reverse than Russian tanks.  After firing from ambush, the western tank can backup quickly behind a building, trees, or smoke. The can then reposition to another location (ideally preplanned) to fire again.

There is a big advantage for a drone to be positioned behind a tank. The drone operator can call out the azimuth to the approaching Russian tank, letting the Ukrainian tanker keep the barrel toward the enemy, waiting for an open shot. The azimuth for the friendly tank would be close, need just minor adjustments when the gunner actually see the Russian tank. Teamwork makes the Dream work! lol

comments.text:
Hearing that Russia is sending more wounded to the Frontline is rather telling of how desperate they are for manpower. I've been searching trying to find any examples of such a tactic being used in war and I can't find a single one. Almost every historical example is purely defensive with one of the only exceptions being the Japanese in WW2. Even then though the Japanese would only send out the wounded who could fight on a Banzai charge. The type of wounds Russian soldiers are being sent out with would have seen a Japanese soldier left back at base with a rifle and a few grenades, expecting them to fight to the death.

I can't even find any records of the Soviet Union getting that desperate. It's truly something unique to history and utterly horrifying

comments.text:
Remember- in a largely static war of attrition, in which the overwhelming amount of casualties are the result of artillery (now including drones, which have taken a major role, but in which the volume is still in the favor of Russia), the side firing up to 5x more artillery per day (during the Battle of Bakhmut, most sources claimed an average of 60k v 12k rounds per day) is 'not' taking more casualties.

Any claims of 'the attackers taking more casualties' is bunk. Consider: 1941 Operation Barbarossa; 1937 Sino-Japanese War; 1980 Iran-Iraq War; US Invasion of Iraq; Battle of Stalingrad; 1937 Battle of Shanghai. All examples show the attacker suffering fewer casualties than the defenders, with the advantage being the volume of ordnance (artillery, armored vehicles, airpower [and now drones]), all of which Russia has and still has a massive advantage in terms of volume.

Also: lol, 'human wave tactics'. Yeah, the Germans tried using this excuse to explain their loss in WW2, but Enemy At The Gates is not a reliable source.

The rapid transition to a market economy led to economic collapse, hyperinflation, mass poverty and the rise of oligarchs who took control of state assets. This make Ukraine’s pursuit of NATO membership not just understandable but maybe necessary, to secure its sovereignty and future. Today, the U.S. and its allies hold the upper hand. comments.author: @Saor_Alba
comments.text: I was born in Scotland, to a Scottish mother and an Irish father, 36 years ago my youngest daughter married an American soldier and is now an American citizen living in America with a large family. I have visited America many times over the past 30-odd years and until today I always regarded the American president as the leader of the free world. I can no longer in good faith say I still believe that, in fact, I don't even regard Trump or his administration as an ally but rather an adversary. Today I listened to the man who is set to be the new German chancellor make an unprecedented scathing speech about Trump and America, and an uncharacteristically direct statement from the UK Prime Minister, for the first time in my life, as a child of post-war Britain, I regard Germany more as an ally than the USA, something I never ever thought I would hear myself say. If America can lose my trust and respect, just think how others less amenable to the USA must be thinking. Under Trump, America has lost its way and has alienated every single ally it had, and sadly I don't think it will ever recover.

comments.text:
$9 million per tanker trip doesn't sound like a lot of money, until you realize that those tankers are not VLCCs (supertankers).  It suggests the Russians are making hardly any extra money at all now by selling via the shadow fleet -- the ship charges are eating all the margin between the world oil price and the Russian oil price cap.

"A total of 28 tankers loaded 21.48 million barrels of Russian crude in the week to Jan. 26." -- according to gCaptain.  That's 770,000 barrels per tanker.  (A VLCC is 2 million barrels.)  At $9m per trip, that's $11.70/barrel of extra cost, quite a bit when crude is at $71 and the cap price is $60.  Typical worldwide shipping costs are around $3 per barrel.

BUT: who owns that shadow fleet?  It's a bunch of Russians, of course.  So the excess money over the price cap has shifted from the Russian oil companies to Russian tanker fleet owners, but it's all still going into Russia.  The fleet operators are probably not taxed as effectively as the Russian oil giants, so there is some loss of revenue to the Russian state.

So what is the remaining incentive for oil buyers in India and China to buy uncapped Russian oil?  It used to be they'd pay e.g. $68/barrel, saving a few bucks off the market price, and Russia would get $65/barrel, making a few bucks over the price cap.  They were only buying at $68 because the Russians refused to sell any oil at $60.  But now, with no incentive left, the Indians and Chinese will threaten to go back to non-Russian oil supplies unless Russia sells at the capped price.

replies.author: @amnfox
replies.text:
@fireteamomega2343 Agreed. I get annoyed when people act like Putin is some James Bond villain bent on world domination.

This is geopolitics, and NATO has played several hands over the years that have poked the bear. Putin is no saint—he’s definitely not the hero of this story—but NATO does bear some responsibility for the actions he felt he needed (or needs) to take to secure Russia’s future.

Take Georgia in 2008—NATO had been pushing for Georgia and Ukraine to join, despite Russia warning that this would cross a red line. When Georgia moved to reclaim South Ossetia, Russia invaded, sending a clear message: NATO expansion into former Soviet states would be met with force.

In 2014, Ukraine was caught in a tug-of-war between the West and Russia. When protests (some Western-backed) led to the ousting of a pro-Russian president, Russia annexed Crimea, home to its strategic Black Sea Fleet. Again, NATO had been discussing Ukraine’s eventual membership, fueling Russian fears of being boxed in.

Now, in Ukraine, similar dynamics are at play. NATO armed and trained Ukrainian forces before the war, expanded missile defenses in Eastern Europe, and refused to rule out Ukrainian membership. From Russia’s perspective, this was an existential threat—especially given NATO’s past interventions in Serbia, Libya, and Iraq, showing that Western promises of restraint don’t always hold.

It’s honestly hard for Americans to relate. We’re geographically isolated, with two of our biggest trade partners (Canada and Mexico) on our borders. We don’t share land borders with direct rivals, nor have we spent decades fighting proxy wars or staring down a nuclear-armed opponent right next door like Russia has with the West.

comments.text:
Thank you for the video, Wyrm, a very nice animation style and information provided made me enjoy it from start to finish. 

I would like to express my opinion on the topic of the economy, as I find that the information presented in the video might improve from it.

Concerning "no signs of economic slowdown" statement, I advise checking Vladimir Milov, a Russian economist that does Sunday review of the current economic situation in Russia, or some of the Central Bank of Russia reports. The Russians currently have issues with inflation and high interest rate, as well as signs of speculation in the banking sphere. Moreover, attacks dealt by the Ukrainian drones are dealing serious damage to the long-term income for the Russian oil. One thing Russians are good at, however, is hiding the information about their economy by blocking information outright or fabricating numbers.

Ukraine, meanwhile, is being bankrolled by the EU countries and international humanitarian organizations, alleviating some pain from the conflict. It was also able to recover pretty much 1/4 of its GDP (as you've shown yourself) in a situation where there was a massive exodus of the population, a large chunk of the country is occupied and a lot of people serve in the military. One thing to also point out: the grain corridor works. Ever since the invention of the suicide naval vessels, Russia doesn't dare to show itself in the Black Sea nor to try to prevent merchant vessels from entering and leaving Ukrainian ports. Mine hunting missions, organized by Bulgaria, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine made it a safe route to traverse.

To conclude my point, I think that the economic warfare should be considered undecided as well.

P.S. The farmer protests that have been mentioned in the video were either organized by the Russian sponsored activists and organizations (like in Poland); occurred in already unfriendly to Ukraine but friendly to Putin Orban's and Fico's governments; have already subsided thanks to the EU intervention in the form of additional subsidies (like in Bulgaria).

P.S.S. Donal Trump is slowly shifting the deciding status of the US in this war away from his country and closer to Europe, meaning The Global Chessboard could also shift to the EU vs. Russia contest, where the EU is clearly unlikely to support them.

replies.text: I remember that. That was back during 1994 when Bill Clinton was still in office and Boris Yeltsin was in charge of Russia. That deal, which was to be honored by the U.S by ALL future presidents was to protect Ukraine, resulting in Ukraine handing over tons of arsenal (before that, they had the THIRD biggest arsenal in the world). Looking back at that,  the 1994 Ukraine president Kuchma should have never gone along with that deal. While Yeltsin was a nice guy, Putin is not (Putin has stated that he didn't want to honor the ruling that Yeltsin had set in place and threw it out). I know Clinton has expressed regret in recent years about doing that 1994 deal because of recent events. In a nut shell, Trump asking for this mineral deal actually goes AGAINST the original deal that happened during 1994 (something he isn't allowed to go against) and Putin broke the agreement set up by Yeltsin. Putin broke it as early as the late 2000's / early 2010's (he was violating the agreement many years before 2022, especially during 2014), so he's in the wrong as well (and just mentioning that since Trump keeps throwing blame on Ukraine when they are NOT at fault in this situation at all and are instead stuck between two sharks: Trump and Putin).

replies.text:
Not many facts here, rather more his opinions, and I don't think his plans are remotely realistic. There are basically three options, 1. give Putin what he wants (not sure why that is so terrible as it is basically what the people who live in the affected area want); 2 carry on the current stalemate indefinitely; 3 arm Ukraine to the hilt and start world war 3 (now quite possibly with the US and Russia on the same side). 

I'm not defending Putin, he shouldn't have invaded, but Ukraine and the west have no claim to the moral high ground, after all the west has started far more wars in foreign countries than Russia. Remember this all started when the west overthrew the democratically elected (pro-Russian) government of Ukraine in 2014, a fact which whilst widely reported at the time, seems to be largely brushed under the carpet now for some reason. 

Also, I don't believe there is a scrap of evidence to think Putin wants to expand any further than the Eastern territories of Ukraine that he now largely holds. Russia's only military interest (other than supporting allies) has been areas like this, former parts of USSR populated by Russians who retain family, business and cultural links with Russia.

What the west needs is to become friends with Russia again. I think that is what Trump wants - whether he succeeds remains to be seen - but clearly the current approach is a disaster so surely he should be applauded for trying something different?

Mr. Sanders,

As a European, I am speechless about what is happening to the USA. The last time a politician used phrases like those of Mr. Trump was in 1934. And we all know what happened next.

As a German citizen, I still experienced how sirens were regularly tested to warn the population in case of an nuclear attack by the Warsaw Pact. In close proximity, Nike missile systems were installed to destroy enemy bomber formations.

What always gave us courage was knowing that we were not alone—having friends who shared the same interests and ideals. That now seems to be over. Now we have a neo-Soviet Union again, and our friends have either abandoned us or are in the process of switching sides.

What has become of humanity?

replies.author: @a0flj0
replies.text: Just a month or so ago it was expected for Pokrovsk to fall - after Russia spending several thousand troops, maybe as much as 20K or 30K, for taking it. If Pokrovsk doesn't fall, and instead turns out to be the turning point of the war, that's better than expected. Ukraine was prepared to cede even more territory, retreating while causing unsustainable losses to Russia, and most likely wasn't expecting Russia to fold already. Plus, it's just a very small Ukrainian gain - Russia might scramble some more thousands of poor souls and send them to die in Ukraine and still take Pokrovsk. But there are already signs that Russia is at least very close to out of fuel, even if possibly not yet completely.

replies.author: @Pedro-bk1ic
replies.text:
@@a0flj0 Yep.  Russia doesn't appear to have the resources to keep fighting at this pace through the duration of 2025.

But they've also been pushing Ukraine back since Avdiivka.  We don't know what state their forces are in, and whether they are close to collapse.

Both sides looked winded, but Ukraine may have done a better job picking their battles.

replies.author: @Third-Kind
replies.text: At this stage, I'm sort of reminded of the final year of WW1. In 1918, the Germans tried to throw in everything they had through the Spring Offensive, and while they made some significant progress, the German forces were left completely exhausted afterwards, allowing them to be pushed back by the Allies (completely with semi-fresh manpower and weaponry through the USA) between August and November. I can already see parallels in that Russia is showing signs of exhaustion, while Ukraine is holding on through foreign support. (Though whether the USA continues to support Ukraine is completely up in the air right now no thanks to Trumpty Dumpty.)

Dennys, I suggest you have a look at what NATO is without the USA.
The NATO countries without the USA is quite powerful and rather a sleeping giant that nobody should wake up.

So YES, NATO is extremely strong together with the USA.
But NATO without the USA is still so much stronger than Russia, even should the US decide to leave, it would be a suicidal mission for Russia.

NATO without USA has more active soldiers than USA, Russia and China combined and a higher GDP than Russia and China combined.
So NATO without USA is not really weak as some like to portray it.

Hey Denys,
ABSOLUTELY CORRECT about Ukraine having its nuclear arsenal restored.  The best model for doing what needs to be done is likely Israel.  How does Israel get its nuclear weapons?  They use a Dimona reactor which was built with the assistance of France back in the 1960's.  This reactor is plutonium production reactor.  If France helps Ukraine build its own plutonium production reactor, then Ukraine will be able to become self-sufficient in terms of building its own weapons.  And between the time that reactor would become operational until there is sufficient production capacity to build new nuclear weapons, France or the UK could provide the necessary fissile materials.  Building the warheads themselves is something that Ukraine can handle.

That said, maybe Ukraine should start building the warheads now in anticipation of having the fissile materials provided and/or produced later on.

comments.text:
I want Ukraine to have peace and security, but I understand the US point of view.
The purpose of an alliance is to make all members safer.  The idea in adding a member to an alliance is that the strength that the new member adds to the alliance more than balances out the additional risk and liability of having to defend that new country.
Over the last few decades NATO membership has expanded from 12 members to 32. The addition of 20 countries in Europe has somehow not enabled Europe to be able to take effective action independent of the United States.  However it has added millions of square kilometers and hundreds of millions of people to the US's security responsibility.
Ukraine is a devastated country currently at war with Russia.  It is clear how strongly it is in Ukraine's interest to join NATO.  What's not clear is how it is in the United States' interest.  The US may accept responsibility for Ukraine's security anyway, but I don't understand the criticism against the country for having reservations about it.

comments.text:
The geopolitical trajectory of the Russo-Ukrainian conflict has been shaped by deep historical, strategic, and security considerations, making its outcome largely foreseeable. At the core of Russia’s unwavering stance lies its perception of Ukraine as an inseparable part of its historical and civilizational identity—a sentiment rooted in the origins of Kievan Rus, the medieval polity often regarded as the foundation of Russian statehood. This historical narrative, reinforced by centuries of imperial and Soviet-era integration, has cemented Ukraine as a space Russia is unwilling to relinquish, particularly in the face of Western influence.

The conflict, however, was not an unavoidable course of history but rather an outcome that could have been averted through diplomatic means. In late 2021 and early 2022, the Russian Federation formally proposed negotiations with the United States to address what it perceived as an inequitable post-Cold War security arrangement in Europe. Moscow’s grievances stemmed from the unfulfilled assurances given during the 1990 reunification of Germany, when Western leaders, including U.S. Secretary of State James Baker, implied that NATO would not expand "one inch eastward." However, NATO's successive enlargements—incorporating former Soviet republics and Warsaw Pact members—were perceived in Moscow as a direct encroachment on its sphere of influence and a fundamental breach of trust.

Despite Russia’s overtures for a renegotiated European security framework, the United States and its allies dismissed these concerns, operating under the assumption that post-Soviet Russia lacked the military and economic strength to enforce its strategic red lines. This miscalculation proved to be a critical factor in the subsequent escalation. Viewing Ukraine’s deepening alignment with the West—particularly through military cooperation and NATO aspirations—as an existential threat, Russia launched a full-scale military intervention in February 2022.

The war became the battleground for a larger geopolitical confrontation, with the United States and NATO committing extensive military, financial, and intelligence resources to Ukraine. The Ukrainian leadership, emboldened by Western support, pursued maximalist objectives, believing that Russian forces could be defeated on the battlefield. However, the strategic realities and the asymmetry of interests in the conflict ultimately dictated its outcome. For Russia, the stakes were existential; for the West, they were primarily geopolitical. As history has demonstrated in conflicts where a great power perceives a war as vital to its national security—such as the Soviet determination in World War II or the U.S. in the Cuban Missile Crisis—the commitment to victory is unyielding.

In the end, the inevitable unfolded. Russia, leveraging its superior strategic depth, military-industrial capacity, and political will, secured its objectives, reshaping the geopolitical balance in Eastern Europe. The conflict underscored the failure of Western policymakers to recognize the fundamental nature of Russian strategic imperatives, a failure that, had it been addressed through genuine diplomacy, could have averted war altogether.

comments.text:
Insights
1. Critique of Strategic Narratives: The analysis exposes how moral and political rhetoric can be deployed to justify a prolonged conflict—even when peace might be achievable through early negotiations.

2. Interdependence of Technology and Sovereignty: A core insight is that technological self-sufficiency is not merely an economic goal but a critical factor in maintaining national and geopolitical independence.

3. Multipolar World Implications: The discussion underscores a significant transition in global power. As unipolarity gives way to multipolarity, traditional alliances and strategies may no longer serve the security needs of all nations.

4. Missed Diplomatic Opportunities: By sidelining diplomacy, the West may have inadvertently reinforced the conflict's escalation, illustrating how short-term strategic choices can have long-term destabilising effects.

5. Corporate Influence on Policy: The intertwining of corporate interests with state policies reveals potential risks where economic ambitions might override broader security considerations, thereby deepening international rivalries.

Meanwhile, new power structures will emerge, with China, the Global South, and regional blocs playing more decisive roles in global affairs. Whether peace brings stability or new tensions remains uncertain, but one thing is clear—the world order as we knew it will never be the same.

comments.author: @suroot
comments.text:
We have failed to be a true friend to those who have believed in the United States. There is no cost-saving justification for this betrayal. The billions spent in recent years seem to support Ukraine have been funneled not into securing peace, but into the United States ultimately surrendering to Russia, all while hindering Ukraine’s ability to stand on its own and repay the United States and Europe for their past assistance.

By abandoning Ukraine at this critical juncture, we’ve allowed Russia to regain strength and influence, creating a more dangerous geopolitical environment. The resources and economic potential that could have been used to help Ukraine rise as a robust, independent partner for the West have instead been handed over to an adversary.

During the American Revolution, France and Spain helped the American colonies in their struggle against Britain. France provided significant military and financial aid, while Spain offered support through indirect military action and resources, although it did not officially recognize the U.S. or sign peace treaties. 

It is impossible to ignore the historical parallels between Ukraine’s struggle for independence, their choice for Democracy and the early days of the United States. The U.S. would not have become the nation it is today without the crucial support of foreign powers, like France and Spain, during its fight for independence. France provided significant military aid, including troops, naval support, and funding, while Spain helped by providing resources, supplies, and indirect military action, particularly in the southern territories. Without this foreign assistance, the outcome of the American Revolution would have been uncertain.

In the same way, Ukraine has fought for centuries to preserve its sovereignty and identity, first against the Russian Czars and later the Soviet Union. Yet, when the moment came for Ukraine to finally secure its independence—facing the threat of cultural and territorial erasure—the United States, a nation that owes much of its early existence to foreign support, has turned its back on Ukraine.

The United States made promises to Ukraine in exchange for its nuclear disarmament, offering security guarantees that have not been honored. As Ukraine faces relentless aggression from Russia, the U.S. has faltered in its duty to stand by its allies, choosing geopolitical convenience over the values of democracy and self-determination. It’s hard not to see the hypocrisy in this. If the United States had never received foreign support during its early fight for independence, it may never have even existed as a nation. Yet now, when another nation seeks that very same independence, the U.S. hesitates to honor its promises.

Ukraine’s fight is not just its own; it is a fight for the principles the U.S. was built on. The U.S. must not forget the debt it owes to those who stood with it when it was struggling to forge its future. It’s time for the United States to live up to its commitments and stand by those who are fighting for their freedom, as others once stood by the U.S. in its most desperate hours.

Ukraine sent Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) personnel to Iraq as part of the U.S.-led coalition after the invasion in 2003. Ukraine contributed forces primarily for peacekeeping duties, and the Ukrainian military was stationed in the southern region of Iraq, particularly in the area around Al-Qadisiyyah province. Ukrainian forces participated in both combat and stabilization missions alongside other coalition forces, including U.S. soldiers. In short, Ukraine has been a U.S. ally seeking NATO membership, and the United States made a promise to provide security guarantees, and a path to join NATO, if it surrendered its nuclear weapons, which it did. However, the United States has failed to honor its promises to Ukraine.

The U.S. Has Abandoned a Friend in Favor of an Adversary: A Betrayal of Ukraine’s Sovereignty

The United States made a promise to Ukraine. In 1994, Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons in exchange for security assurances under the Budapest Memorandum. In return, Ukraine trusted that the U.S., along with the U.K. and Russia, would guarantee its territorial integrity and sovereignty. Fast forward to today, and those promises have been shattered.

In a disturbing turn of events, recent statements by U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth suggest that Ukraine must now surrender its territories to Russia, with NATO membership deemed “unrealistic.” These comments are not just a shift in policy—they are a betrayal of Ukraine, a nation that trusted the U.S. to honor its commitments.

Ukraine’s willingness to abandon its nuclear weapons was based on a fundamental belief that security guarantees from major powers, including the U.S., would protect its sovereignty. Instead, the U.S. has abandoned a friend—a nation that has stood with Western values—and chosen to appease an adversary, Russia. This decision effectively allows Russia to achieve its strategic goals by force, with consequence for the United States. The U.S. is now signaling that it values diplomatic shortcuts and appeasement of Russia over its historical commitment to a democratic ally.

By suggesting that Ukraine should forgo its territorial claims and abandon its aspirations for NATO membership, the U.S. has not only failed Ukraine but has failed the very principles it claims to uphold. This is not just a foreign policy failure; it is a violation of trust and a blatant disregard for promises made.

Instead of standing firm with a nation that disarmed in good faith, the U.S. is caving to an authoritarian regime that is openly violating international laws and norms. Russia, the aggressor, is now seeing its territorial ambitions legitimized by the very nation that once pledged to support Ukraine’s sovereignty. This dangerous shift undermines not only Ukraine’s future but also the credibility of the U.S. on the world stage.

Ukraine has sacrificed its security in favor of peace and diplomacy. But instead of receiving the support it was promised, it is being asked to give up more and more in the name of a peace that favors Russia’s expansion. This marks the moment when the U.S. has abandoned its principles and its friends, and instead chosen appeasement over standing firm for democracy and sovereignty.

The U.S. now risks sending a dangerous message: that promises made in the name of security are negotiable when it becomes inconvenient. This move doesn’t just jeopardize Ukraine—it undermines the trust of all U.S. allies and partners who might one day question whether the U.S. will stand by its word.

As the West continues to debate its course of action, the most pressing question remains: How long can the U.S. abandon its friends in favor of appeasing its adversaries before it irreparably damages its standing on the world stage?

This is negligent leadership and a failure of vision. Every inch of territory conceded to Russia not only emboldens the Kremlin but strengthens its strategic position, particularly in terms of access to vital resources and geopolitical influence. By allowing Russia to reclaim these territories, the West is handing Russia the means to recover its losses, which in turn will make it an even more formidable adversary.

As Russia regains these resources—whether energy, minerals, or strategic land—it will bolster its economy and military capabilities, effectively enabling the country to take a step closer to being a direct competitor to the United States on the global stage. The consequences are profound: by giving in to Russian aggression now, we are setting the stage for a more dangerous future, one where Russia is more capable, more confident, and more assertive in its global ambitions.

This policy of appeasement is short-sighted. The surrender of land and sovereignty doesn’t lead to lasting peace; it fuels further instability. History has shown that when aggressors are allowed to expand without facing consequences, they only grow bolder. This is how the seeds of future conflicts are sown. The West’s failure to stand firm today will inevitably result in more wars in the future—not just with Russia, but with other rising powers who see that aggression pays off.

The wealth of resources in the territories being conceded to Russia is worth trillions—a vast treasure trove that could have fueled Ukraine’s growth and transformation into a strong economic and military partner for the West. These resources, ranging from energy reserves to precious minerals, would have provided Ukraine with the means to build a thriving, self-sustaining economy, one capable of not only repaying the United States and Europe for their assistance but multiplying that investment several times over.

Had Ukraine been supported in holding onto these lands, it could have joined the Western world as a prosperous and resilient nation, with the resources to stand on its own and contribute meaningfully to the global economy. The integration of such a strategically important and resource-rich country into the West would have strengthened Europe and the U.S., both economically and militarily, creating a partnership with Ukraine that could have countered Russia’s aggression more effectively.

replies.author: @amandarhodes4072
replies.text:
This war has also reinforced the legacy understanding of drone warfare at the same time. Current or next gen tanks and IFVs already have active protection systems that can neutralise drones and the Javelin ATGM. Something that the 1st gen Abrams and baseline Leopard 2 that are in Ukraine are not equipped with.

These features are on the KF-51, Abrams-X, Challenger 3 tanks. So while not all of these are going to be build in large numbers the systems in question already exist.
The Russian tanks in Ukraine are 60-80 years old now so are simply not built to defend against modern weapons.

Drones are not a new thing in warfare. They have been used to great effect in Iraq, Afghanistan and the middle east. Serving as surveillance and long range assassins.
Thing about drones is that they don't work well in enclosed conditions like in a town or amongst trees as they have poor situational awareness. Drones in Ukraine are used mostly in open fields for this reason. Wireless drones can be jammed with good electronic warfare equipment. Fibreoptic guided drones can't be jammed but have much shorter operational ranges.

You can jam a drone but can't jam a human. Humans also have the ability to distinguish between a target in amongst bushes or buildings. Something that even modern AI struggles to do. Cameras can only do so much for visibility if you are not here on the battlefield in person.

comments.author: @Meower68
comments.text:
In early China, it was determined that horse-mounted cavalry were vulnerable to arrows and catapult-launched bolts (darts / arrows / spears, depending on the size of the catapult). They came up with something which would stop them. They gave the cavalry something which looked like a large silk bubble. When you're riding at a trot (or faster), airflow through the entry point would cause the silk (as lightweight as possible) to billow out into a large balloon behind the rider (and, to some degree, the horse). An arrow / bolt hitting that bubble will not penetrate; it will cause the bubble to collapse at the point of impact. But this slows the arrow / bolt enough that it won't penetrate the armor the rider is wearing.

Putting sharper tips on the arrows / bolts meant that they ripped through the bubble and still killed the rider. Alternately, firing a volley of arrows / bolts, spread out over a couple seconds, meant that the first ones to land collapsed the bubble and the later ones were not slowed, so they did the job.

ERA, cope cages ... it's all modern variations on the same principle. Disperse enough of the energy that they can't penetrate the armor. The Javelin has a two-stage warhead to trigger off the ERA, exposing the armor underneath, then penetrate the bare armor. These rounds are kinda like the sharper arrows / bolts, in that they go through the countermeasures and aren't materially slowed by them.

comments.text:
There is so much nonsense in this video, here are some things worth mentioning and please google it yourself.
1. Cope cages are slat armor, it´s nowhere documented that it was supposed to be Against the Javeline or NLAW. 
2. Slat armor does not work by exploding the RPG warhead prematurely, it destroys it´s fuse mechanism. The idea is the narrow cage squishes the tip of the RPG round and short circuits the fuse. It is effective only against this one type HEAT warhead. A HEAT round being exploded prematurely is a little bit effective but the effect is rather small, which can be seen when a JAVELINE or NLAW strikes a tank from over 1m distance, it still penetrates.
3. The late cages aren´t against RPG´s either, they are against drones in general. It has nothing to do with their spacing and so on, as I already have described in point 2. 
4. The frag munition either has a platter charge and fragmentation function or fragmentation only. I don´t see any platter charge, only frags. This does not mean there isn´t any. But all your animations and pictures show frag. In this case the animation where the frag is mounted to the drone is wrong. It´s 180 deg. turned.
5. EFP´s have less penetration but travel way farther while still haveing decent penetration compared to HEAT charges. You can look it up in various charts. Those are used in mines and artillery pieces.
Just because somebody has a big YouTube channel does not mean he knows what he is talking about.

One of the biggest blunders Russia did when they escalated the war in February 22 was to not do proper SEAD. replies.author: @Efeye-s
replies.text:
@@Ratman2025 SEAD stands for Supression of Enemy Air Defense. Though what I believe the original poster was referring to is DEAD, which stands for Destruction of Enemy Air Defense. It's a complicated subject, but SEAD could for instance be when you employ a lot of radar-seeking missiles that forces the enemy to turn off their radars and hunker down, or use a lot of jamming so the enemy radar screens is just a big mess and they can't make sense of whats happening. Both of these are temporary, so when you stop SEAD the enemy still has their air defenses intact. There are also lots of different ways to counter this, so proper SEAD is very difficult to do and can be disatrous if you get it wrong. DEAD is when you actively hunt down and destroy enemy air defense, so it is permanently destroyed. This is what the first commenter said was Russia's mistake, to not destroy the Ukrainian air defence when it was unmanned and vulnerable.

For Russia to destroy the Ukrainian defence systems now they have to A: Know where they are and B: have something they can hit it with. Air defence stays a bit back from the frontlines and is constantly moving around. A missile that has both long enough range and is accurate enough to hit a single vehicle-sized target is extremely expensive, and Russia does not have a lot of those missiles. So even if Russia know exactly where the target is and launch a missile, by the time the missile arrives Ukraine could have moved it out of the way, so Russia just sent a very rare and expensive missile to hit a patch of dirt.

comments.author: @StephenSipe
comments.text:
Paul, your comprehension on battlefield tactics and Tactical Operations at Company Level and lower is excellent. Your analysis of Operational Level schemes of maneuver and impact on Strategic Level planning is much weaker.  For example, Ukrainian Operational Level schemes of maneuver are to expand their depth of control around Sudzha. Most Offensive Operations have been Battalion Level probes to capture the next major village or tree line. If the Russian defenses crumble, the have a Company or 2 at the rear of a Battalion push to do an internal Battalion battle handover to capture the next major village, or tree line and stopping only at major water features. 

The Ukrainian Military Intelligence Officer is probably looking at the calendar and the forecasted weather out to March. This is usually the beginning of the muddy season. So whatever is secured now, is probably terrain which can be defended until May. 

The Ukrainian Eastern Flank is far different. Even with their best Units engaged, Russian Offensive Operations at the Operational Level are spent. The drone only Tactical Level Operations are really part of Strategic Level testing.  Ukrainians are trying to develop an Operational Level scheme of maneuver starting with tactical use of drones, to breach Russian minefields in depth and enable a Strategic Level breakthrough. I am surprised drones have not been used as MICLIC launchers and then to deploy another dragged charge to proof a lane. 

The Eastern Operational Level Offensive Operations are to prune Russian over extension of their front lines. The place where Ukrainians will launch a major Combined Arms attack is yet unknown. These smaller Offensive Operations are helping to train up additional Units with experience to form up a Corps Level Offensive Operation. This will not be Strategic Level, unless successful, and followed up with an Exploitation Of Success Offensive. This may involve enveloping a large Russian force.

Permit me to provide a larger context.
1.  When the action started in 02/22, the Ukraine was spread thin. It had to defend the border against Belarus and the entire border with Russia and the occupied areas by separatists.
2.  By blowing he 13 bridge crossings to Belarus, fortifying that border with a kill zone of a few miles and Belarus giving its armor to the RF, the danger there was reduced.  But you still had position troops.

Yo, this is wild!  This soldier, Kevin Vinje. He is from the same area as I am, in Norway.  More precisely Ulefoss, Telemark, Norway. 
I was good friends with his cousin, and his cousin's girlfriend.       It's safe to say, me and him didn't see eye to eye back then. 
It's along time ago though.

I first saw him, and knew he was going to Ukraine on Norwegian news.
  More precisely. he was there un the attack on the foreign soldier training camp or barracks, outside Lviv.
So it was in the beginning of when the foreign soldiers first started coming to Ukraine. 

Trust me. That he went from, like me, a small town boy, that went to parties in the weekends and in general was around cars and country, like all of us are in small towns, and to what he is now.  
I would never have guessed man. I did NOT see that coming. 

But man... he changed.  It's so freaking cool that he did go to Ukraine, and how he went from messing around to having a.. or should I say THE purpose.
Not just thinking abt doing something, but doing it too!    I'm really proud to have someone representing our area, doing this. Not many would. 
Like I said, i would never think he would be someone doing it.  

I'ts inspiring to say the least. 

Kevin -  Så jækla rått! (So freaking awesome!)

We, Ukrainians, are grateful to Kevin and the other men and women from the North. They have undoubtedly taken a great step, one that we respect and for which we are thankful. When we talk about war, especially in Ukraine, it is important to remember that we, Ukrainians, and the peoples of the North, though distant, are still relatives through different lines of history. Today, we are part of a vast world facing enormous challenges.

In our shared history, there are many moments, like those in the songs about Olaf or Prince Oleg, that show how deeply the destinies of our peoples are intertwined. A true war is a struggle of all nations, each of us standing for our land, our culture, and our loved ones. And while everyone has their own motives and decisions, we must all understand that this war is not just about territories but about what defines us as human beings.

comments.author: @floridasoldat
comments.text:
Chris- you were right when you speculated the structure of foreign units may be more complex than you explained. GUR’s International Legion is indeed separate from the original, standard International Legion. Then you have a multitude of other units and entities with their own versions of international legions (Azov just recently announced the formation of their own IL, 3rd Assault Brigade recruits, trains, and utilises lots of foreigners under their own formats, and at least when I first arrived in Ukraine at the beginning of 2023, Karpatska Sich also employed a significant number of foreigners). 

Then you also have regular Ukrainian brigades under different branches that may employ smaller numbers of foreigners in more isolated, specialised units. For example, after leaving the International Legion in 2023, a group of us formed an assault company (Chosen Company) under a regular Ukrainian storm/infantry brigade (the 59th Motorised Brigade). Chosen operated both as our own assault element under the 59th as well as part of larger initiatives alongside the Ukrainians in the 59th while we were part of that brigade. While part of the 59th, we served under the Ground Forces, and were not part of the International Legion.

replies.author: @ariew503
replies.text:
@@Zappina Hey, i just wanted to point out that I think you may wanna reconsider your statement about pain tolerance in women compared to men. Men tend to have higher pain thresholds in lab studies. That means it takes more stimulation for them to start feeling pain. And many studies suggest that men tolerate more pain in controlled settings (e.g., cold pressor test).

However, women often outperform men in real-life pain scenarios (e.g., childbirth, chronic pain endurance) and like the video stated, our blood clots up faster then men's, and this is a side effect of our bodies being capable of birth. It is also true that many women function under significant pain for extended periods, showing high pain endurance and resilience. This means being able to endure pain is more valuable than being able to perceive pain at a slower rate in a combat scenario. Because eventually if you get shot, your going to feel the pain no matter what, but to be able to endure that pain and survive is what matters most.

1. During the Volhynia tragedy (1943), not only Poles were killed, but also Ukrainians. One of the main reasons behind the conflict was the oppression and humiliation of Ukrainians by Poles.

replies.text:
Specifically, you’re quoting Brad Pitt’s version of the character from the movie Troy.  That’s an important distinction to mention.  Achilles said no such thing in the Iliad.  In Homer’s epic, his conflict with Agamemnon was not over the king failing to fight his own battles but with his decision to seize Briseis, who Achilles considered to be his prize of war.  Essentially, it was a dispute over property, with Achilles feeling outraged by the king’s theft.

“And now you threaten to strip me of my prize in person –
the one I fought for long and hard, and sons of Achaea
handed her to me.
My honors never equal yours,
whenever we sack some wealthy Trojan stronghold –
my arms bear the brunt of the raw, savage fighting,
true, but when it comes to dividing up the plunder
the lion’s share is yours, and back I go to my ships,
clutching some scrap, some pittance that I love,
when I have fought to exhaustion.
No more now –
back I go to Phthia. Better that way by far,
to journey home in the beaked ships of war.
I have no mind to linger here disgraced,
brimming your cup and piling up your plunder”

-Achilles, the Iliad, Book 1, lines 190-202.

comments.text: I'm from Kharkiv and had to move out to protect my then 10 month-old child. My parents and in-laws are still there. They don't want to leave their homes. In your video I saw the streets where I used to drive to work, the cafe we used to go to with my colleagues, that big shopping mall where we used to buy staff for our house, my husband's office that was also demolished. It made me cry so hard. And I'm thankful to you for this, because I was holding this im myself for a long time and now I'm crying and it feels better. Thank you so much. Thank you for telling our story. I hope soon this terrible war finishes and you come to make a video about wonderful peaceful Ukraine. replies.text: Similar to my girlfriend too. My girlfriend is from Kharkiv and fled in April 2022 to Russia. She’s of mixed Ukrainian Russian heritage and had family in Russia who housed them temporarily. She said that upon arrival, she had to register herself and they tried to confiscate her Ukrainian passport and tried to force Russian citizenship upon her. She also got some harassment from Russian people who were constantly giving her abuse, she got her car vandalised for having Ukrainian plates, got physically assaulted by an older man and got called a nazi which required her to have stitches on her lips. After that her family (4 of them) decided to leave Russia for good. They converted all their money to dollars and drove from Voronezh to Latvia where they stayed for 6 weeks in emergency accommodation. She eventually got asylum status accepted in the UK and all 4 of them live and work in Northern Ireland now. She used to be a secret dual citizen of Ukraine and Russia but now she hates Russia/russians with a passion.

comments.author: @sergeyd5777
comments.text:
Drew, I gave your presentation a like when I started watching it, but later withdrew it. Please do not get me wrong.
Whoever was directing this project is a questionable professional.
I understand your desire to show the message of resilience. The message of life and hopes. And you did that by yourself, actually being there, thank you!
But look at the final product! Your video shows fine lives of ordinary Ukrainians, cozy cafes, entertainment and peace. You show some damaged buildings, very selectively, and some memorials. And the scariest thing you demonstrate is the sound of a siren...
Where are the crimes of war, the razed to the ground towns, massive genocide and the horror of war? Where is the report about everything that is really happening in Ukraine? Ruined lives, the doctors and first responders in the civilian areas, the stories of the soldiers? Everybody knows it is there, I am a Ukrainian and I am in constant touch with my close people over there right now.
I think the presentations like yours give the reason to many EU and US politicians to question the very need to help Ukraine in any serious way, and such opponents are numerous. They simply say, "Why help, just look at these scenes of happiness and normal life that Drew Binsky just brought from over there!"

No matter your intentions and personal effort, I think that as a messenger you've failed very big on this project.

comments.author: @musehtaicho
comments.text:
So for the context, here is summary of yt 52 min "interview with Yakut" soldier callsign Tuta. There may be some mistakes in timeline as I wrote it from memory, not rewatching to check. 

On Nov 16 2024 - two of them [Tuta and Geek] had mission to enter village Trudovoe north of Ugledar on bike and place a flag. Bike was damaged by drone drop, so they proceeded on foot. They did not know that building they choose for placing flag was in fact Ukr command post. His comrade was off right there, while he managed to reach cover. Two ukr soldiers followed him, he got one and hid in a shed where second ukr tried to persuade him to surrender (actually stalling for time for FPV to reach them).
After hand to hand happened, he took radio from ukr soldier, put a nade under his vest and after checked him in a head. Took cover in a basement with two enters and heard in a radio that after him ukr sent another 6 soldiers. They surrounded basement and began calling him - he remained silent. Then they threw few nades one after another through both entrances while he ran rounds trying to avoid shrapnel. First ukr soldier who was ordered to check on him was off on spot. More nades followed. After that smoke. Tuta soaked his cap in water and covered face. Another volunteer who decided to check on him was shot, but thanks to low visibility survived and was dragged out crying "I am 300!" After that they tried to set basement on fire, but water in 5L bottles were stored inside and he somehow managed. Nobody tried to storm him after that.

5 a.m. Tuta left basement thankfully not guarded and hid nearby. At morning ukr came back to drop into basement another batch of nades and shoot RPG into each entrance. After that they left. Tuta contacted his commander and recieved new task - recon and sabotage. Hiding at day he scouted area at night and found house where ammo and weapons were stored, house with other goods - clothes, drones etc,  and  yard with fuel. No guards at all. He took plast-d from storage and cooked fuel storage - he was afraid that will reveal him but ukr reported to command that storage was hit by 122mm. That emboldened him and he set material storage on fire - that is when on radio enemy agreed that Yakut survived and somewhere there. 
At least 10 people and APC was sent for clean up. Tuta hid in a munition storage - prepared RPG - he found RPO-A Shmel but was not trained to use it so decided not to, also tried to prepare MG but his old wound from May 9th 2024 reduced ability of his right hand so instead he prepared few AKs. When group passed by, he shot APC near engine knocking it out with RPG and opened chaotic fire with AK followed by nades. Enemy fled and reported via radio that Yakut somehow recieved reinforcement. 

On Nov 18 russian forces tried to storm village with armored column but were stopped by drones and bombarded by 120mm mortar. As hesitant as he was, Tuta could not bear hearing in radio screams of his comrades so he left hiding and found mortar position - crew of 3 did not notice him so he finished leader and gunner, ammunition bearer tried to raise hands, but anyway...
At night he tried to fall back, but was spotted by thermals and hit multiple times by drones. He was forced to hide back in a village. Once again he left building before morning and hid nearby. Group of ten arrived, hesitant to go in - all of them in civilian clothing, hiding weapons and vests. Probably to avoid russian drones. Two women amongst them - one said "We hit him hard with drones, he bled out for sure" - young guy literally sniffed the door and said "Yeah, I think he is done". They left. 

Tuta decided to leave by daytime (he had a dream of his wife and kid and time on his phone was 14:28, while irl his phone was damaged long ago) - easier to avoid drones. People passed 10m nearby while he was hiding in grass and mud. He crawled about 500m until taking refuge in a burned MTLB. Inside he found dead russian soldier a bottle of water and a "Snickers". He decided to wait a day or two until rain stops. There he had another dream - all his 5 kids shivering from cold, and eldest son told him "We cant stay, we need to move". So he left his cover next day and continued to crawl through the fields, avoiding treelines as they are point of interest for drones. At some time russians made another attempt to storm village and all focus was on armored column (damaged MTLB where he was hiding was also hit by arty). Tuta used it for a run. Some shots were fired his way from column also. 

His friend offered to pick him up on a bike, but that would mean focus of FPVs so Tuta refused, but asked to make double shot every half an hour so he could keep direction crawling in tall grass. 
It was about 500m to hangars when he noticed drone above him. He picked radio "Hey, pal, is that you above me?" - "No! That is not ours, run!" As he dashed to the nearby hangar, drop exploded behind him and another later in front of him. That was last on that drone, so Tuta showed few international gestures and reached safety.

Aside from 3 knife wounds he got in close combat, he also got 14 shrapnel pieces from drone strikes. Some of these were removed some left inside due


Also few additions: 
Whole operation took him 6 days and he barely had something to eat as his supplies were in a backpack of his comrade shot first. 

They were second pair to enter village - first fell to drones. And his first dream was about his dead comrades walking area and showing him "Look, here is danger zone where they got us" - when he woke up he remembered that they were hit in a complitely different area. But when he tried to leave village he was wounded around place they showed him in a dream. So in his interview he concluded: "Spirits of our ancestors do not leave us in a time of need and try to warn us through our dreams". That is why he followed two other dreams I mentioned above. 

While he was running fields and drones were flying above him to armored convoy he tried to shoot them and took down one Baba Yaga. But from the direction of convoy started shooting at him (or at drones) and he decided not to try join them or positions in a treeline as he was covered in mud - to avoid friendly fire.

When he reached buildings on outskirts he heard voices inside and could not grasp what language it was, as it was windy outside, but for sure not russian, so he quietly passed by - uncertain if that may be ukrainean foreign mercs. Turns out that was his friends speaking yakutian - those who made warning shots for him. 

He was not aware of bodycam video until his brother showed it to him. He could not watch it in full as it was too difficult to relive that fight again, also was surprised of how long it was - he remembered barely a minute of that fight. Also could not remember what exact words they exchanged with ukr soldier but reviewing record concluded: "He also a human, a warrior fighting for his motherland, just as I am. Somehow, anyway... we have to keep some humanity [in us]".

On Jan 11th he was awarded "Hero of Russian Federation".

Newspaper "RG" asked him to comment on his award:
"There are hundreds of such fights across the front, but only few are made public."
"I was lucky and survived, they call me a hero. But why is that "Geek" who was killed in same battle is not a hero? Many guys on a frontline everyday perform a feats nobody heard of. This video surfaced and that is why I was awarded so fast. But not a word about "Geek" who was with me on that last mission. It is unfair."  - he asked journalist to write about his friend. 
"Geek" - Anton Timofeev 38yo yakut, father of 3, volunteered in 2022, survived Artyomovsk [Bakhmut], was heavily wounded in 2023 but his friend covered him. So he reenlisted after hospital to repay the debt to his comrades.

Weird story.
My dad was in the Korean War.
Near the end of the war, he wad was put in charge of chinese and North Korean POWS. He was a nice guy and gave all the POWS cigarettes & sandwiches before moving them out. One day they had a russian POW, a Mig pilot who had been shot down by a Sabre Jet. comments.author: @Filoshik
comments.text: On 2:07 they show the Military ID of a presumably NK soldier. Well, this is a standard Russian military ID card in which it clearly states the place of birth ("Место рождения" in Russian) (page on the right; entry number 1) of this soldier which is Tuva, Russia. In Russian it is written as "Тыва", so you can go to 2:07 and confirm it yourself. Tuva is a remote Russian republic in southern Siberia. While their looks may resemble Koreans, they are Russian nationals. Or we can assume that this document is not this soldier's document and was added by the editors for pure aesthetics, in which case the video still lied to us. Be ready to fact check everything that is shown and told to you, otherwise don't watch or listen at all. If you can't read Russian or Ukraine, you can use Google Translate app on your phone to translate any text from a photo.

replies.author: @ashe1.070
replies.text: Read the Geneva Conventions, and the Hague Convention. So, many people like you call many things a “war crime” without having any clue about what the actual laws of war are. Running combatants over with any vehicle isn’t a war crime. It doesn’t matter if they’re running away. You can be taking a dump 100 miles behind the front line, and still be a legally valid target. You don’t need a weapon in your hands to be considered a legitimate military target either. Any member of a belligerent military regardless of that member’s role, or what they’re doing at any given moment is a legal viable target as long as they aren’t surrendering, or seriously wounded. The only exception to this are medical personnel depending on the circumstances. If a medic, or military doctor has a weapon they are a legitimate target to the opposing forces.

replies.author: @magnashield8604
replies.text: @AstroGremlinAmerican  I'm going to agree to a point. But the tanks really had an effect later in 1918. The first arrival of the tank was at the Somme in 1916. Just like the first use of poison gas was at Ypres. Both sides completely underestimated the initial effect. By the time they had grasped the scope of the battlefield utility, the element of surprise was gone. The Germans had effective anti-tank doctrine with artillery and the first anti-tank rifles by the time the British and French were able to mass armor. That is not to say that Armor was not an advantage, it was, but not nearly to the extent that it would have been, properly masses in 1917, rather than tested in 1916, giving the Germans a chance to adjust. The German withdrawals of 1918 was more a realization by the general staff that they could not hold the overstretched lines gained in spring, more than it was a resounding success of the allies punching through. The German army no longer had the ability to continue the fight more than a battlefield defeat. What America really contributed was the backing of material support that would allow the allies to continue the fight. Again, more of a reflection on economic output than actual battlefield prowess.

comments.author: @wattlebough
comments.text: Bradleys are IFVs not APCs. They’re a different and heaviest class of armoured vehicle that carries troops in battle. The M113 is an APC with a light aluminium hull and usually a .50 cal heavy MG. IFVs have heavy steel and alloy composite armour and an auto cannon from 20mm like the German cold war era Marder up to 40mm Swedish CV40. 25mm and 30mm are the more common caliber. Often IFVs will have 2x ATGM missiles on the turret along with advanced imaging and targeting optics.

Especially when the different T models reactive armor, in contrast to the Bradley’s, often are useless wax or clay, because the cuts made to fund the Russian kleptocrats.
Although Bradley’s are effective and there likely are a zillion more American viewers, I would like to see how the CV90s donated by Sweden and others manage.  I would suppose they are used in more hilly and forested regions, like those in Sweden they originally were designed for… and more snowy and muddy conditions.

I have had a privilege to talk with a finnish WW2 veteran about trench storming. (confirmed kills = many) Two lessons I learned from him: 
1) You can not have too much hand grenades with you. (and also back then it was very desirable to have a submachine gun instead of a rifle, because our poor governement could not equip everyone with automatic guns)
2) You can not hesitate in any moment. Trust for the guy next to you is crucial. Too introvert men lost their life in those years at the frontlines against russians.

From my (finnish) military training point of view, this is pure evolution. We all humans learn the ways to keep us alive in any conditions.  Glory to all ukraine fighters! I suppose though, the russians are acting likewise. They also are human beings, evolving to survive. I truly hope this war to end. Without embarrassing the heroes of Ukraine... And if for political reasons this will happen, we are ready in Finland. Welcome.

The only reason Ukraine were able to go so deep is because they picked a region along the border which was  of no strategic importance and was sparsely guarded by a few raw recruits and home gurd equivalent. Ukraine keeps sending troops into the region to replace those that are being lost each day. Russia will see this as favourable because Ukraine is losing a steady stream of troops, specifically in that area.
And for those doubting any of this, look at the maps and look at the losses. comments.author: @Swissvistas-fz9ey
comments.text:
Anyone out there wondering what nuclear war looks like is well advised to watch the 1983 movie "The Day After". It's the end of everything, full stop. The nuclear deterrent is what kept the former Warsaw Pact countries and the West from going to war for that very reason. It is probably fair to say that the present increasingly dangerous  geopolitical situation has its origins in Western arrogance displayed versus Russia after the demise of the Soviet Union, and US political meddling in Ukraine, which started well over ten years ago in the context of intended NATO expansion right up to the Russian border (Victoria Nuland, anyone?). The US de facto created a reverse Cuba Crisis situation on Russia's doorstep.

All this clearly does not justify Putin's brutal war in Ukraine, but the crucial question as to where the loyalties of the populations in the eastern parts of Ukraine lie, will need to be resolved, ideally by means of a democratic referendum as part of a peace treaty. What is uncertain at this point is whether Putin indeed has expansionist plans to conquer other former Iron Curtain countries if he succeeds in Ukraine, or whether that assumption is merely in the fearful minds of NATO strategists. 

What is certain is that Putin and his devoted supporters will never give up on the Russian areas in Ukraine, and the West will need to carefully ascertain whether it's really worth taking the risk of triggering a nuclear war because we pushed things a little too far - regardless of the moral superiority of needing to assist Ukraine. The Russians are proud people, and their tolerance is being tested. IMO, Ukraine will eventually have to give up Russian-speaking territories either because of a military fait accompli, or because the populations living there decide to become part of Russia after a referendum. The concept of realpolitik still applies, regardless of who is wrong or right.

replies.text:
​@@Imperialbbuilding Idk, it's the first real full-scale modern war in a European scenario. Two big armies clashing, no militant insurgency or "anti-terror mission". 

My great uncle told me a lot about his time as a young soldier at the Eastern front during WW2, and this gives me an idea about how he felt. I think as Westerners, we don't have any idea about the brutal conditions in this scenario. The sheer landmass makes every major victory feel like a minor step forward. Keeping the supply lines going is just a hassle and quickly leads to miscalculation and death. The lack of cover in those open fields makes you vulnerable to air attacks. The weather, the endless grey, the mud, the hot summers... It's just a beautiful and yet brutal environment.

comments.text:
For everyone: This is not a MG3, this is the MG42/59, the 7,62x51 mm chambered version of the MG42 by Beretta, Whitehead Motofides and Franchi for the Italian army. Production started in 1959. Ukraine has received several thousands of them from Italy,as Italyis phasing them out in favour of the FAL Minimi. 
Ukraine has also received several hundred MG3 from Germany, but these with the armored vehicles APCs and tanks. Often these are the MG3A1 version, for the fixed moint in Marder and all of the Leopard versions. 
By bad luck, we can not see the fire suppressor, the MG42/59 has still  the thinner one of the original MG42, than it would be far easier to identify/to recognize by everyone.

Pak přiletěl nový velvyslanec USA Andrew Schapiro...o 2 měsíce dříve, než bylo plánováno, protože jeho akutně vzniklým úkolem bylo okamžitě v tom Česku postavit vyděšené a zmatené politiky a média do latě. 
Jediný prezident Zeman ho následující dva roky nepustil přes práh Hradu...
V dnešním multipolárně rozděleném světovém řádu je nutné respektovat geopolitiku každé jaderné supervelmoci. Vynucují si to především USA, proč by k témuž nemělo právo Rusko, Čína, Izrael, Indie a Pákistán, každý podle své síly a velikosti. Pokud se geopolitika nebude respektovat, nemůže být klid a mír. I takto vojensko-politicky rozdělený svět může dobře prosperovat v alespoň relativně zdravém konkurenčním tržním prostředí. Historie to již prokázala mnohokrát... ale právě díky menšinovým leč vlivným mocenským vrstvám v této civilizaci vždy docházelo k narušování klidu. A to jsou přesně ti, s nimiž by si to svět měl okamžitě vyřídit hned, jak o sobě dají takto vědět. Škoda, že OSN je jako neplodná žena, která sama sebe považuje za "mír udržující matku" této civilizace.

No a ještě cítím, že musím důrazně ☝️ upozornit, že v životě jsem nečetl a neposlouchal žádné medium ruské či proruské propagandy. Naopak můj názor a přesvědčení jsou založené právě na osobních zkušenostech a poznání během vývoje této strašné historie a to VÝHRADNĚ z oficiálních českých médií a médií USA či západní Evropy. No a doplňuje mě i dokumentární naučná tvorba z amerických "satelitních" tv programů. 
Realita je totiž taková... všichni v onu chvíli, kdy se "něco děje", informují PRAVDIVĚ  a  REÁLNĚ. 
To proto, že vlastně ani nemají důvod, až na výjimky, informace fabulovat. Nikdo předem neví, jestli se to v budoucnu ukáže jako dobře či ne. No a pokud budoucí události ukáží, že by ta historie mohla nadělat nějakou paseku v současnosti, tak se prostě rozjede informační kampaň fabulací. S nějakými deseti roky, v době, kdy jsou lidé, především mladí lidé zahlceni informacemi a pitomostmi z internetu, to tak velký problém není. A morálka jednoduše neexistuje ☝️
A dělat si starosti se starší generací pamětníků...?? Proč, už toho moc nezmohou a přirozeně stejně ubývají...

Ať je americký prezident sebevětší buran, tak pokud dokáže ti válku ukončit... navzdory všem jejím zastáncům, tak už jen kvůli tomu jeho zvolení není marné. On ale udělá víc... nakopne restart Evropy, která tak zlenivěla a tak si zvykla spoléhat se na Washington, který je od WWII v Evropě stejně jen kvůli svým zájmům a s ní i mnoho dalších zemí a institucí, které si zvykly sát z těch "amerických cecků" bez práce. Trump jako byznysmen chce být prezidentem především pro Ameriku, pro americké voliče. Chce Ameriku, která je po uši v dluzích a pravidelně bojuje s hrozbou státního bankrotu, opět postavit na pilíře mocnosti No.1.
A je mu... vlastně s ohledem na pouhé 4 roky před sebou, mu musí být úplně jedno, jestli to Bruselu, jeho členům či nějaké zkorumpované Ukrajině a především americkým "Demokratům", kteří toto vše punktovali jako pomstu Putinovi za znárodnění firem a institucí v r. 2000, kam je Jelcin v obrovském počtu pustil...vadí.
Trump potřebuje pro své plány byznys. Byznys s celým světem a to včetně Ruska. Ne všechno má Ukrajina na svém území. 
I EU se dříve či později vrátí k obchodu s Ruskem. Vždyť ještě v r. 2014  např. Německý obchod byl až ze 40% s Ruskem. A už teď ti pozorní vnímají, jak moc ty sankce a snahy Putina (skrze užitečného idiota Ukrajinu) zdiskreditovat a přinutit Rusy se ho zbavit, ten vyspělý západní svět poškozují.

Mercenaries are trained to carry more weight and even still... Do you even know half of the things he are carrying?? They are what makes him really reliable.

Logistics is for resupply, you don't need resupply if you have plenty more to work with. And with 520 rounds, that's 15+ mags, which is not even that much when you consider being in a war against endless foes. If he ends up in a long firefight, most of them mags are getting used, plus he literally said depending on the mission, he brings different amounts.

Speed isn't even that important in war as you make it seem. Speed is something that is effective in war, but there will still be times where you have to ditch speed for efficiency... leaving a fast carrier vehicle that is used to bring reinforcements to the battlefield for heavier armored and gunned vehicle that is closer to the fight as an example.

Lastly... Wtf is ease, like no disrespect, but what the hell are you referring to when you state "ease," if your talking about ease of access to do things like move around or use equipment, its the equipment itself that would deal with that, and usually the equipment accounts for when people have more than usual

title: Which Weapons Are Winning and Losing the War in Ukraine
description: The war in Ukraine has seen an array of weapons, from Soviet-era relics to cutting-edge tech, shaping the battlefield. This video ...

comments.author: @arzoo_singh
comments.text:
Counter argument with balanced and honest unbiased points .
1. Precision of Russian Missiles: It’s true that U.S. intelligence initially reported a high failure rate for Russian precision-guided missiles early in 2022. Factors like technical flaws, electronic warfare (EW) interference, and Ukraine’s defenses played a role. However, by 2023, Russia had adapted its tactics, focusing more on strategic targeting of Ukrainian infrastructure. This adaptation significantly improved its operational effectiveness, a point confirmed by some military analysts.


2. Shift in Russian Strategy: After setbacks in 2022, Russia refined its logistics and targeting, particularly on Ukraine’s critical infrastructure, adapting to countermeasures and shifting tactics. Both sides have shown flexibility, adjusting their approaches as the war has evolved, so judging the effectiveness of either side's strategy depends on the phase of the conflict.


3. Zircon and Hypersonic Claims: While Ukraine has claimed to intercept some advanced Russian missiles, evidence of intercepting a Zircon, a true hypersonic missile, is currently lacking. Given the challenges these missiles pose to even the most advanced defense systems, such a claim would be difficult to substantiate without substantial proof and likely serves more as a morale booster than a verified success.


4. Tanks vs. Light Vehicles: Both Abrams and T-90 tanks are highly advanced, but drone warfare and portable anti-tank systems (like Javelins and NLAWs) have shown the vulnerabilities of even the best tanks. In urban and asymmetrical warfare settings, versatile light armored vehicles like Bradleys and BTRs have proven highly effective. This suggests that while tanks have a role, they’re no longer the game-changers they once were without combined arms support.


5. Russian Missile Effectiveness: Early criticisms of Russia's missile performance were valid, but missiles like the Iskander have since proven their effectiveness, especially against critical infrastructure. Recent strikes have damaged or destroyed high-value assets, including some Patriot systems, suggesting Russian missiles are far from ineffective in key operations.


6. The "Cheap vs. Flashy" Narrative: Characterizing Ukraine’s weapons as "cheap but effective" and Russia's as "flashy, expensive, and unreliable" oversimplifies the situation. While Ukraine has indeed relied on cost-effective tools like drones, it also depends on expensive Western assets like Patriots, HIMARS, and Storm Shadows. On the Russian side, even less sophisticated weaponry has shown effectiveness in certain contexts, proving that destructive capability isn’t always tied to cost.


Is Russia Really a "Paper Tiger"?

1. Uneven Support: Russia entered this conflict largely isolated, with minimal early support, while Ukraine has had continuous backing from over 30 nations, including advanced NATO members. Assessing Russia's performance without accounting for this disparity paints an incomplete picture.


2. Essentials of War – Weaponry, Manpower, Supply Chains: Russia has had to rely on its own industrial production and stockpiles, whereas Ukraine’s access to Western supply chains has given it a clear advantage in adapting and sustaining operations.


3. Technological Gap: Russian technology is often compared against the combined capabilities of many advanced Western nations. With access to tools like satellite intelligence, HIMARS, and Patriots, Ukraine has an edge that goes beyond what a single nation would typically counter.


4. "Paper Tiger" Misconception: Labeling Russia a “paper tiger” implies its military is all appearance with no substance. However, Russia has endured under intense pressure, adapting and managing a prolonged conflict. This resilience is significant given the numerous logistical and strategic challenges it faces.


5. Self-Reliance vs. Collective Support: Russia’s reliance on its domestic industrial base—under sanctions—is a stark contrast to Ukraine’s foreign aid. Building weapons, managing logistics, and replenishing losses independently is a considerable challenge when facing the coordinated support of multiple advanced nations.


6. Evolving Alliances: Support from countries like Iran, North Korea, and China only materialized later, and it doesn’t match the volume or technology Ukraine has received from the West. This disparity further highlights Russia’s resilience rather than indicating inherent weakness.


These points illustrate why calling Russia a "paper tiger" doesn’t capture the full picture. The conflict has underscored Russia’s ability to sustain and adapt its war effort despite facing an alliance with more extensive resources and technological advantages.

replies.text:
@@boomer19450 "War does not determine who is right - only who is left."

So morals versus the idea it's another's fault... The result is the same in both instances, though. That said, depending on how you look at it, one might also conclude it's actually the smart thing to do.

If you go, you're pretty sure to have your guts torn out in some muddy trench, if you flee, you can build up your life and raise a family and live your life. I know in *every* war it's always depicted as something existential, to rile up the people, but I'm just not buying it.

I'll be honest here: no-one could ever convince me to fight on the frontlines for no amount of money or no politicians egotripping frenzy - not unless every last one of those politicians was fighting at the front themselves. And even then. I guess one needs to be young and naive, because I, for one, know very well it's a huge waste and an effort in futility. You only have one life, there is no use in wasting it for either money or some ideological illusion.

That's only my take, of course, and I'm well aware other people have other opinions - which I think are delusional and certainly irrational. But to each his own. And I would venture that those that flee have a better rate of survival that those that don't. So it kinda sorts itself out, in a darwinistic sense.

Never forget (hopefully) the mercy shown to him.
I have read such stories of WW1 and WW2.
Small bits of humanity shown tend to not get forgotten. They get passed down to the next generation.
I read one story where an American pilot in WW2 got separated and lost in thick clouds over Germany. He was initially relieved to a bunch of aircraft and he joined in thinking it was his flight.
Welp. Suddenly the sky was clear and he realized to his horror he had joined an entire flight of Germans in formation.
He knew he was screwed.
Apparently the Germans realized this too, started talking on their radios…..and laughing at the dumb American in their mist.
After a bit a German flew next to him, and signaled him to get out of there, they were letting him go (laughing while gesturing).

There was a code in the air at the time.

Look up when a German Pilot escorted a barely flying B-17 home…..
